New Delhi: Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson Sonia Gandhi has asked Prime Minister Narendra Modi to “forgive himself” for his 2017 remark against former prime minister Manmohan Singh, in which he had said Singh knew “the art of bathing with a raincoat on”.

Referring to the recent Supreme Court ruling upholding the Central Bureau of Investigation’s (CBI) clean chit to the former prime minister in the coal block allocation case, Gandhi has written in an article in The Indian Express that there was a “witch hunt” against Dr Manmohan Singh. “The lobby against him was coordinated and well-organised, with actors stretching from the bureaucracy to the media, the judiciary, civil society, and most certainly to the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Today, their bogus crusade has come to its inevitable conclusion of nothingness. Dr Singh has been vindicated on every count,” she wrote.

Gandhi referred to PM Modi’s ‘raincoat’ remark against his predecessor as the lowest point of parliamentary history, and sought an apology, citing his recent Instagram video where he forgave students for using “abusive words” against him.

“It is not a coincidence that the Prime Minister was also among the most vocal proponents of the attack on Dr Singh. His snide and atrocious remarks in the Rajya Sabha on 8 February 2017, that only Dr Singh knew ‘the art of bathing with a raincoat on’, will go down as the lowest point of our parliamentary history. Since Mr Modi is these days ‘forgiving’ India’s students for attacking him, perhaps he can take this opportunity to forgive himself for his undignified slander against Dr Singh,” she wrote.

Gandhi’s comments come after the Supreme Court’s 29 July judgement upholding the CBI’s clean chit to Singh in the alleged coal block allocation scam. The court also pulled up the trial court for rejecting the CBI’s closure reports and making adverse observations against Singh without a “compelling reason”.

Gandhi further wrote the campaign questioning his integrity involved sections of the bureaucracy, media, judiciary and civil society, as well as the RSS and BJP. Gandhi also accused the Modi government of misusing the Enforcement Directorate (ED) and CBI to pressure political opponents.

“Leaders are either silenced through coercion or cynically folded into the BJP or, in some remarkable instances, rewarded with ministerial positions as well. When credible accusations of corruption emerge, the Modi government simply brushes them aside. Corrupt when you’re in the Opposition, suddenly clean when you jump ship!”

She also pointed to the economic growth during Singh’s 10 years as prime minister, along with rising consumption and private investment. Gandhi said the United Progressive Alliance (UPA) government recorded higher economic growth than the following 12 years and argued that millions of people were pulled out of poverty during the period.

“Dr Manmohan Singh’s government heralded profound economic change with unprecedented rates of growth and a consumption and private investment boom that propelled us into the ranks of middle-income countries. In 2008, when the global economy faced turbulence and collapse, India demonstrated its resilience. During his tenure, the shift in employment patterns became very discernible with lakhs moving into higher-productivity occupations. Over the last decade, however, this diversification has been reversed.

Based significantly on the programmes put in place in the previous government and the acceleration in growth rates, India decisively began winning the battle against poverty and deprivation. Let us not forget that in spite of the re-working of how the growth of India’s GDP is calculated, the 10 years of the UPA government saw higher economic growth than the past 12 years, resulting in millions being pulled out of poverty.”

Gandhi said Singh’s “statesmanship, erudition, and fundamental decency” were “sorely missed in today’s conflicted times”. His record, she said, was increasingly being recognised as a period of “decisive economic, political, and social advancement”.

She also listed the Right to Education Act, Other Backward Caste (OBC) reservations in centrally funded higher education institutions such as the Indian Institutes of Tehchnology and Indian Institutes of Management, the Forest Rights Act, Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) and the National Food Security Act, 2013, among the major measures of the Singh government.

On MGNREGA, Gandhi wrote that it was the “most powerful social security intervention”, pointing to its role during the Covid pandemic in reaching poor and vulnerable sections. She said the National Food Security Act was another major avenue through which the government was able to provide basic food rations to crores of families.

Gandhi also drew a contrast between the democratic environment under Singh and the present government. “Politically, the Dr Manmohan Singh decade as prime minister was characterised by the growth and strengthening of democratic institutions of the state and civil society. Dr Singh heralded a new era of transparency in government through the landmark Right to Information Act (RTI), which enabled citizens to access the government’s inner workings. The RTI now stands totally emasculated. There was an explosion of independent media, which was characterised by a fearlessness that appears more remarkable when juxtaposed with its current enfeeblement.”

“Civil society emerged as a force to be reckoned with, and our students had the freedom to protest against the government and even the prime minister, without being fired upon by metallic pellet guns or AK-47s,” she added.

She also pointed to Singh’s record of engaging with Parliament and the media, noting that he held more than 100 unscripted press conferences as prime minister. The Indo-US nuclear deal was another major achievement, she said, ending decades of nuclear discrimination against India and marking the country’s arrival on the global stage. “We all certainly regret that he is not here to see this day,” Gandhi said, adding that it was nevertheless a solace that Singh’s prediction from January 2014 was becoming increasingly evident.
History, she said, would remember Singh as “a quiet, gentle but a most consequential prime minister”.

“As far as this particular agreement is concerned, we are examining its implications, both from the perspective of our national security, as well as considerations of regional peace and stability,” Jaiswal said.

When Pakistan and Saudi Arabia concluded their mutual defence pact in September 2025, the Indian government said it would take all steps to protect the country’s national interests and ensure comprehensive national security in all domains, reflecting New Delhi’s concerns over the development. Saudi Arabia’s growing military proximity to Pakistan against the backdrop of the West Asia conflict has not gone down well in New Delhi, people familiar with the matter said.

A joint statement issued by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye on Friday said the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement builds on shared strategic interests and longstanding defence cooperation. The pact also reflects the shared commitment of the three countries to strengthen their collective security and promote peace, security and stability in the region.

“The agreement is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression, and stipulates that any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all. It further provides for the enhancement of all aspects of defence cooperation among the three states,” the joint statement said.

Jaiswal responded to separate questions on events organised in different part of the world to mark the “independence” of Pakistan’s Balochistan province and the violent protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) by urging the world community to hold Pakistan accountable for human rights violations and atrocities.

“We continue to follow developments across the world. At the same time, I would like to highlight that we have seen the kind of human rights violations that were committed in PoK and other parts of that country. We call on the international community to hold Pakistan accountable for its misdeeds, abuses and flagrant violation of human rights, including of all its people,” he said.

Over the past few months, large-scale protests in PoK related to elections to the local assembly had led to a situation where “public discontent was answered with bullets, blackouts, repression and oppression”, Jaiswal said. More than 90 people were killed and many more injured in the violence, and the international community needs to hold Pakistan to account for the mass violation of human rights, he said.

Jaiswal said that there has been no change in India’s policy towards Pakistan. “We are where we were earlier. I need not emphasise which country is responsible for cross-border terrorism and which is the epicentre of terrorism, and where the action lies for stopping cross-border terrorism,” he said.

Mamata Banerjee faced 'chor, chor' slogans during a TMC protest in Kolkata over remarks on Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose made by a BJP leader.

TMC chief Mamata Banerjee on Tuesday faced "chor, chor" slogans in Kolkata during a party programme held to protest controversial remarks about Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose by a BJP MP. The disruption came just two days after Banerjee was met by similar protests in Halisahar, adding to the political tension around her public appearances.

The TMC programme had been organised around alleged derogatory comments on Netaji, but it turned into another confrontation as a group gathered near the venue and raised slogans against Banerjee. BJP leader Nagendra Roy's remarks have given the TMC an opening to present the issue as an attack on Bengal's nationalist legacy, while the protests against Banerjee have shifted attention to allegations of corruption and public anger.

Banerjee reached Shyambazar five-point crossing in north Kolkata carrying a portrait of freedom fighter Khudiram Bose and paid tribute at the feet of Netaji's statue. The programme was organised by the TMC over remarks made by Roy, popularly known as Ananta Maharaj.

The controversy began after Roy described Netaji as a "war criminal", questioned his leadership and raised doubts over the role of the Azad Hind Fauj in India's freedom struggle. West Bengal BJP leaders later distanced themselves from the statement, saying Roy's comments were personal and were neither endorsed nor believed by the party.

FSSAI bans plastic, foil packaging for pan masala under new rules
Moving forward, pan masala can only be sold in eco-friendly packaging or traditional rigid containers.

India’s food safety regulator, FSSAI, has updated its packaging rules to ban plastic and foil packaging for pan masala. Under the new Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Amendment Regulations, 2026, manufacturers can no longer use plastic-based materials, plastic laminates, aluminum foil, or metallised layers to pack pan masala.
Moving forward, pan masala can only be sold in eco-friendly packaging or traditional rigid containers.

The new rules have been notified as the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Amendment Regulations, 2026 and will come into force from the date of their publication in the Official Gazette, according to a press release.

What packaging will be allowed?
Under the amended regulations, pan masala can be packed using paper, paper board, cellulose or other naturally derived materials.

That said, these materials must be completely free of plastic, including polyethylene, polypropylene, polyester, polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and other synthetic polymers, copolymers or laminates. Tin and glass containers have also been listed as permitted packaging materials for pan masala.

Plastic waste rules will also apply
The amendment further states that relevant provisions under clauses (f) and (i) of Rule 4(1) of the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, will also apply to pan masala packaging.
The FSSAI issued the amendment under the powers granted by the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, with the prior approval of the Central Government.
What other plastic packaging is banned?

India already prohibits plastic sachets used to store, pack or sell gutkha, tobacco and pan masala under the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016. The latest FSSAI amendment specifically lays down permitted materials for pan masala packaging and excludes plastic-based and plastic-laminated materials.

Earlier, the government completely banned plastic sachets used for storing, packing or selling gutkha, tobacco and pan masala under the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016. The Plastic Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011 prohibited the use of plastic sachets for storing, packing or selling gutkha, tobacco and pan masala. They also said plastic material in any form could not be used for packing these products.

India also prohibits plastic carry bags and plastic sheets below 50 microns under the Plastic Waste Management Rules. The rules were introduced in 2016 and increased the minimum thickness for plastic carry bags from 40 microns to 50 microns.
Plastic wrapping or packing films around sweet boxes, invitation cards and cigarette packets are also prohibited under the Plastic Waste Management Rules.

Pan masala's plastic packaging banned; FSSAI mandates paper, tin or glass

The FSSAI has targeted the plastic used in pan masala's packaging. Under the new rules, pan masala manufacturers can use only plastic-free paper, paperboard, cellulose or other naturally derived materials, along with tin or glass containers.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has introduced new packaging requirements for pan masala, specifying plastic-free materials that can be used to package the product and ruling out plastic, aluminium foil and metallised layers from the permitted packaging options.
The changes were notified through the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Amendment Regulations, 2026, published in the Gazette of India on Monday (August 10).
The amendment modifies the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Regulations, 2018 by adding pan masala as a new entry under Schedule 4, which deals with the list of suggestive packaging materials.

Under the new provisions of the FSSAI, which comes under the Union Ministry of Health and Welfare, pan masala can be packaged in paper, paperboard, cellulose or other naturally derived materials, but these materials must be completely free from plastic.
The notification specifically states that the packaging cannot contain polyethylene, polypropylene, polyester, polyvinyl chloride (PVC), or any other synthetic polymers, copolymers or laminates.

The restriction goes beyond conventional plastic packaging. The specified paper and naturally derived materials must also be free from aluminium foil and metallised layers. This means packaging that uses a paper-based outer material but contains plastic or metallised layers within the packaging would not meet the material specifications set out in the amendment.
FSSAI has also permitted manufacturers to use tin or glass containers for pan masala. These are listed separately as permitted packaging options under the new entry.
The amendment further states that certain provisions of the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, framed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, will also apply to pan masala packaging.
The regulations come into force from the date of their publication in the Official Gazette. FSSAI notified the final amendment after completing a consultation process on the proposed changes.

The authority had first published the draft Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Amendment Regulations, 2026, on April 28, inviting objections and suggestions from people likely to be affected by the proposed regulations.
The draft was open for public feedback for a period of 60 days.
FSSAI said the objections and suggestions received from the public in response to the draft were considered before the final amendment was issued.
The final notification was issued under the powers granted to FSSAI under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, with the previous approval of the Central Government.
The notification is specifically a packaging regulation.
It does not announce a ban on pan masala as a product. Instead, it adds pan masala to the packaging schedule and specifies the materials that can be used for its packaging.
The new rules therefore place the focus on moving pan masala packaging away from plastic-based materials.

Manufacturers using paper, paperboard, cellulose or other naturally derived materials will have to ensure that these materials contain no plastic, synthetic polymer, copolymer or laminate and do not use aluminium foil or metallised layers.

The other packaging alternatives explicitly listed by FSSAI are tin and glass containers. With the amendment coming into force upon publication, these provisions now form part of the amended Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Regulations, 2018.

Crocodile tears: Dharmendra Pradhan slams Rahul Gandhi over Jharkhand protests

Dharmendra Pradhan accused Rahul Gandhi and the Congress of dodging a Parliament debate on student issues. The clash deepened the deadlock in the House and sharpened the BJP's charge of double standards on youth concerns.

Former Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan on Tuesday attacked Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over the Opposition's stand on a discussion on student issues in Parliament. He accused Gandhi of spreading lies and shedding "crocodile tears" instead of agreeing to take part in the debate.

The BJP then accused Gandhi of shifting the goalposts to deliberately disrupt Parliament.

Manmohan Singh ‘most consequential PM’: Sonia Gandhi says his prophecy on Narendra Modi is coming true
Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson's remarks come days after Supreme Court gave the late ex-PM Manmohan Singh a clean chit in coal block allocation case.

Echoing the late ex-PM Manmohan Singh's words about himself, that history will remember him kindly, Congress leader Sonia Gandhi said on Tuesday that he was a quiet but “most consequential” prime minister that India has had.

The Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson's remarks in an article published in The Indian Express came days after the Supreme Court gave Manmohan Singh the clean chit in the coal block allocation case, one of the many corruption cases of the Congress-led UPA era before Narendra Modi and the BJP ascended to power in 2014.

"The date July 29, 2026, was an important but unacknowledged day in our recent political history as in a remarkable judgment, the Supreme Court upheld the CBI's clean chit to Dr Manmohan Singh in the alleged coal block allocation scam," Gandhi noted.
She said the judgment brings to a conclusion one of the most tragic arcs of our public discourse — “the witch-hunt against Dr Singh, a man of the most remarkable probity and integrity”.

On Modi, Sonia Gandhi said that Manmohan Singh's prophetic prediction of January 2014 was now becoming increasingly self-evident, in an apparent reference to his then statement that it would be “disastrous for the country” to have Modi as PM.

In a more immediate swipe at Modi, Sonia Gandhi further referred to his video in which he said he was “forgiving” students who'd used abusive words against him during the recent protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party that forced a change of education minister. Sonia Gandhi said that since Modi was these days forgiving India's students for attacking him, perhaps he would take this opportunity to forgive himself for his slander against Manmohan Singh.

It was not a coincidence that Modi was also among the most vocal proponents of the attack on Manmohan Singh, she said. “His snide and atrocious remarks in the Rajya Sabha on February 8, 2017, that only Dr Singh knew 'the art of bathing with a raincoat on', will go down as the lowest point of our parliamentary history,” she said.

"The lobby against [Manmohan Singh] was coordinated and well-organised, with actors stretching from the bureaucracy to the media, the judiciary, civil society, and most certainly to the RSS and BJP… Today, their bogus crusade has come to its inevitable conclusion of nothingness. Dr Singh has been vindicated on every count," Gandhi said in her article.

On the SC clean shit, she that, more importantly, the top court pulled up the trial court for rejecting the CBI's closure reports and making adverse observations against the former prime minister for “no compelling reason”.

Manmohan Singh's record of integrity and accountability stands in stark contrast to how the Modi government has operated, so clearly and grossly misusing agencies designed to investigate crime and corruption like the ED and the CBI, she said.

“Leaders are either silenced through coercion or cynically folded into the BJP or, in some remarkable instances, rewarded with ministerial positions as well… When credible accusations of corruption emerge, the Modi government simply brushes them aside. Corrupt when you're in the Opposition, suddenly clean when you jump ship!” Sonia Gandhi wrote.

“Introspection, like charity, must begin from home. Ultimately, the attack on Dr Singh was motivated by a desperate desire to shift the public conversation and narrative away from his outstanding governance record,” she further said.

Manmohan Singh's government heralded profound economic change with unprecedented rates of growth and a consumption and private investment boom that propelled India into the ranks of middle-income countries, Gandhi stressed.

In 2008, when the global economy faced turbulence and collapse, India demonstrated its resilience, she said. “Let us not forget that in spite of the reworking of how the growth of India's GDP is calculated, the 10 years of the UPA government saw higher economic growth than the past 12 years, resulting in millions being pulled out of poverty,” Gandhi said.
UPA's work 'being sought to be amended'

The Manmohan Singh government delivered on the constitutional promise of a Right to Education and expanded social justice through the introduction of OBC reservation in centrally-funded higher education institutes like the IITs and IIMs, she said. “The Forest Rights Act recognised the ancestral rights of our Adivasi and forest-dwelling communities, after a decades-long struggle. The MGNREGA, recently demolished by the Modi government, was the most powerful social security intervention set up anywhere,” she said.

Another signature achievement of Singh's government was the National Food Security Act, 2013, which identified and guaranteed access to basic food rations for crores of families, she said. “This is being sought to be amended. Soon after he demitted office, he had warned that the rights-based legislation would come under assault and his fears have, most sadly, come true,” she said.
Singh heralded a new era of transparency in government through the landmark Right to Information Act, which enabled citizens to access the government's inner workings, she said.

"The RTI now stands totally emasculated. There was an explosion of independent media, which was characterised by a fearlessness that appears more remarkable when juxtaposed with its current enfeeblement," she said.

Civil society emerged as a force to be reckoned with, and our students had the freedom to protest against the government and even the prime minister, without being fired upon by metallic pellet guns or AK-47s, Gandhi said, taking a swipe at the Modi government.
The prime minister regularly made himself accountable to Parliament and to the media through 100-plus unscripted press conferences, she said.

"And of course, we cannot forget that the landmark and path-breaking Indo-US nuclear deal, which overturned decades of nuclear discrimination against and denial towards India and marked our arrival on the global stage, was possible because of his political courage and sustained initiative," she said.

The “mischievous and indefensible” allegations against his integrity have been exposed as hollow, and his record as prime minister is increasingly being recognised for what it was — a period of decisive economic, political, and social advancement in Indian history, she said.

"We all certainly regret that he is not here to see this day and to guide the nation with his wisdom. But it is a solace to us all that his prophetic prediction of January 2014 is becoming increasingly self-evident with every passing day… History will indeed remember him kindly as a quiet, gentle but a most consequential prime minister," Gandhi said.

Her remarks come after the apex court closed the criminal case against Singh by setting aside a summoning order passed against him. The veteran Congress leader, who passed away on December 27, 2024, now stands formally acquitted in the high-profile criminal case.

Cash row: Justice Yashwant Varma inquiry report to be tabled in Parliament today

The enquiry report into allegations against former judge Justice Yashwant Varma will be tabled in both Houses of Parliament on Wednesday. The move sharpens the constitutional question of whether removal proceedings can continue after his resignation.

The enquiry report into allegations against former Allahabad High Court judge Justice Yashwant Varma will be tabled in the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha on Wednesday, bringing a controversial case involving the alleged discovery of burnt currency at his official residence to a crucial stage.

The three-member enquiry committee, constituted by Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, investigated allegations against Justice Varma following the discovery of burnt currency notes at his official residence in Delhi in March 2025.

Following the incident, Justice Varma was transferred from the Delhi High Court to the Allahabad High Court, and his judicial work was withdrawn pending an in-house enquiry. He resigned from the Allahabad High Court on April 9, 2026, while the parliamentary inquiry was underway.
The resignation has raised a key legal and constitutional question over whether Parliament can continue with removal proceedings against a judge who has resigned while the process is pending.

The parliamentary inquiry committee submitted its report to Speaker Om Birla on May 18. The committee was reconstituted in February and comprises Supreme Court Justice Aravind Kumar, Bombay High Court Chief Justice Shree Chandrashekhar and senior advocate B V Acharya.
The proceedings originated after a removal motion signed by 146 MPs was submitted to the Lok Sabha Speaker in July 2025.
WHAT IS THE ALLEGATION AGAINST JUSTICE VARMA?
The controversy dates back to March 2025, when a fire broke out at Justice Varma's official residence in Delhi. During firefighting operations, burnt currency notes were allegedly found at the site.

Justice Varma has denied the allegations and maintained that no cash was recovered from his residence. He was not present at the residence when the fire broke out and subsequently questioned the basis for holding him responsible for what happened at the premises.

Following the incident, then Chief Justice of India Sanjiv Khanna ordered an in-house inquiry. The panel reportedly found prima facie that Justice Varma and his family had control over the room where the cash was allegedly found.

In August 2025, Speaker Om Birla constituted a three-member committee under the Judges (Inquiry) Act to examine the allegations. Justice Varma later challenged the validity of the parliamentary inquiry before the Supreme Court. The proceedings were ultimately allowed to continue.
The committee completed its proceedings after Justice Varma resigned on April 9 and subsequently submitted its report to the Speaker on May 18.
The report will now be placed before Parliament. Its findings could determine what further parliamentary action is considered in the case.
CAN PARLIAMENT REMOVE A JUDGE AFTER RESIGNATION?
This is the central constitutional question surrounding the case.

Under Articles 124 and 217 of the Constitution, a High Court judge can be removed on grounds of "proved misbehaviour" or "incapacity". The removal process requires an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by at least two-thirds of members present and voting, followed by an order of the President.
Justice Varma's resignation, however, has created an unusual situation because the parliamentary removal process was already underway when he stepped down.

Faced with demands to scrap the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, from different corners of the country on Tuesday — including a unanimous resolution passed in the Tamil Nadu Assembly and mass protests in the streets of Mizoram’s capital — the Union government informed its allies and other parties that it would move a resolution in the Lok Sabha on Wednesday to refer the Bill to a Joint Parliamentary Committee, sources said.

Moving the resolution urging the Centre to withdraw the Bill in its present form, Tamil Nadu Minister Rajamohan said the Assembly was deeply concerned by provisions in the legislation relating to the transfer, management, and sale of assets of charitable organisations to the government on grounds such as expiry of FCRA registration, non-renewal or refusal of renewal, cancellation of registration, or surrender of registration. “These provisions may adversely affect the autonomy of charitable organisations and, in particular, the functioning of educational and social welfare institutions run by the minority communities,” the resolution said, urging the Centre to undertake comprehensive consultations with all stakeholders, including State governments.

Fears that Christian institutions will be disproportionately affected by the Bill overflowed onto the streets in Mizoram, one of the three Christian-majority States in the country. Hundreds of Christians from different denominations participated in a rally in Aizawl under the newly formed Council of Churches in Mizoram. The Bill would give a designated authority sweeping powers over the land, buildings, funds, and other assets of churches and NGOs whose FCRA registrations are cancelled or not renewed, without judicial oversight, said R. Lalbiakliana, the council’s president.
The Bill came up for discussion at a meeting of the Business Advisory Committee of the Rajya Sabha, but the government made no commitments at the meeting, despite strong Opposition objections.

According to sources, Union Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju raised the issue at the meeting. Congress general secretary and Rajya Sabha Chief Whip Jairam Ramesh pointed out that the Bill was not on the agenda and said the Opposition was of the view that it should be withdrawn. Trinamool Congress deputy leader in the Rajya Sabha Sagarika Ghose echoed the demand. DMK leader Tiruchi Siva also strongly opposed the Bill. “The FCRA Bill in its current form is unacceptable to us. Sending it to a Joint Parliamentary Committee will not serve any purpose,” he told The Hindu.

Sources said Mr. Rijiju did not make any commitment about the fate of the Bill, despite the Opposition insisting that a decision be taken at the meeting. However, the government later informed allies and other parties that it would move a resolution in the Lower House to refer the Bill to a JPC, according to sources.

BJP MP Sasmit Patra, who attended the meeting as a special invitee in his capacity as a member of the panel of chairpersons, is learnt to have argued that the Bill should be referred to a JPC for another round of scrutiny.

The Tamil Nadu Assembly resolution said that “any amendment must preserve the principles of natural justice, proportionality, protection of property rights, legitimate expectation, and federalism. While ensuring transparency and accountability in foreign contributions, it must protect the rights of legitimate charitable, educational, religious, cultural and social welfare organisations.”
The Bill, introduced in the Lok Sabha on March 25, proposes tighter government oversight of non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and foreign funding in the country.

Among its key provisions is the creation of a designated authority to manage and dispose of assets if an organisation loses its FCRA licence. Under the proposed law, if an FCRA certificate is cancelled, surrendered, or lapses, foreign contributions and all assets created using those contributions would vest in a government-appointed designated authority without any prior hearing or judicial determination.

The Bill also provides that if a fresh certificate is not obtained within a prescribed period, these assets could be sold or transferred to a government department, with the proceeds credited to the Consolidated Fund of India. The existing right to reclaim assets upon re-registration would be removed, and the founding institution would be permanently barred from reacquiring them.

Opposition parties have argued that the Bill disproportionately affects minority institutions, alleging that some of its provisions would restrict legitimate foreign funding for Christian NGOs and minority-run welfare and educational institutions. The government, however, has maintained that the proposed legislation is not religion-specific and is intended to strengthen the regulation of all foreign contributions.

The Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA), which met in Delhi on Tuesday (August 11, 2026), affirmed and endorsed the decision by the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee (CWRC) to direct Karnataka to ensure the release of Cauvery water at the rate of 12,000 cusecs a day from Wednesday for the next 15 days to neighbouring Tamil Nadu.
This means that Karnataka would have to provide about 15.55 thousand million cubic feet (tmc ft), considering that the flow of 11,574 cusecs in 24 hours equals one tmc ft.
Distress and dispute: On Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and the Cauvery

Responding to this, Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar said a decision on the next course of action would be taken after carefully assessing the water availability in the State. He stressed the need to protect the interests of State’s farmers while also complying with the orders of the Authority and the CWRC. He is set to hold a meeting with legal experts and bureaucrats on Wednesday (August 12, 2026) on the possible legal options.

CWMA chairperson Saumitra Kumar Haldar told The Hindu later that Karnataka “is in a comfortable position” to comply with its order. The CWMA arrived at the decision after considering the storage, inflows, and the meteorological outlook for the next seven days, he said.

Earlier, Karnataka appealed to the CWMA to defer any decision on further releases and take a considered decision based on actual hydrological realities at the end of the South-west monsoon season. If not, it pleaded, the CWMA should at least reduce the quantum of water release from 12,000 cusecs a day to 10,000 cusecs.

Karnataka told the CWMA that the Cauvery basin was “reeling under severe hydrological distress”. It pointed out that all four reservoirs in the Cauvery basin had received only 77.746 thousand million cubic feet (tmc ft) of cumulative inflows in this water year, which was “about 47% less” than the 30-year average. Also, the inflows to the reservoirs were rapidly declining, it said.

Karnataka argued that it had already ensured flows of 86,942 cusecs at Biligundlu [the measuring point of Cauvery flow on the inter-State boundary] as against the prescribed quantum of 52,500 cusecs by the CWMA. It argued that the realisation by Tamil Nadu was bound to be much more as additional flows too were in transit

It argued that there was no scope for further water release to the neighbouring State given its own “deficit monsoon, dwindling inflows and limited storage”. Also, there was a dire need to conserve water for drinking and essential uses besides taking care of farmers’ kharif crop.

Karnataka contended that Tamil Nadu, in contrast, was “in an advantageous position” as it already had “sufficient storage” in its reservoirs, besides having the benefit of forthcoming north-east monsoon as well as any downstream flows.
Also read: Why did Cauvery panel order Karnataka to release water? | Explained

The State said that distress sharing must be equitable, while contending that a rigid, predetermined pro-rata formula based solely on inflows into Karnataka’s reservoirs could “disproportionately burden the State”. Karnataka further demanded that a broader system be put in place to assess distress based on the situation across the entire basin, rather than merely on inflows to its four reservoirs.

On its part, Tamil Nadu appealed to the CWMA to direct Karnataka to ensure releases of 37 tmc ft at Biligundlu by August end, taking cognisance of the backlog and the quantum that is due on pro-rata basis from August 13 to 31.

It argued that maintaining the entire one year’s drinking water requirement for Bengaluru as a contingency plan against any worst-case scenario was not justified and should not be used to deny its legitimate share.
Tamil Nadu argued that its basin area experienced a much higher rainfall deficit of 36% so far in this water year, compared with the 9% deficit in upstream of KRS and 19% in that of Kabini.

Tamil Nadu maintained that the present substantial downstream flow to it was largely due to surplus flow from Kabini and contended that despite improved inflows into the KRS catchment, releases from this reservoir had remained low, indicating issues related to equitable sharing of available flows. It appealed to the CWMA to direct Karnataka to regulate releases from both KRS and Kabini.
It argued that Karnataka’s projection of substantial benefit to Tamil Nadu from the north-east monsoon “lacked adequate scientific basis.”

Speaking to The Hindu, the CWMA chairperson said that as “against the long term average of 83 tmc ft in the four reservoirs of Karnataka in the Cauvery basin, the current storage is 77 tmc ft”. Besides, the upper riparian State’s reservoirs would be receiving 2 to 2.5 tmc ft a day at least for the next one week. “It is for this reason that we have decided that Karnataka can spare one tmc ft a day to Tamil Nadu,” Mr. Haldar observed.

While the upper riparian State wanted the Authority to settle for 9,000-10,000 cusecs (0.78 tmc ft to 0.86 tmc ft a day), Tamil Nadu, the lower riparian State, had sought the release of 1.5 tmc ft a day.

Referring to the circumstances under which the CWMA decided on July 30 to go by the CWRC’s position, Mr. Haldar said, “We were not sure how the southwest monsoon would behave. Even the meteorological forecast, both from the Indian Meteorological Department and Skymet, was not positive. As there was a 50% deficit in realisation at Biligundulu, we had asked Karnataka to release about 4.5 tmc ft. But, the rain started from then on.”

As for the need for a “permanent, scientific” distress-sharing formula, Mr. Haldar replied that “given the conditions that characterise the basin, there is no single formula that will work in the case of the Cauvery, as dynamics keep on changing”. However, he had sought views of the riparian States to come up with a formula, the chairperson added.

Senior bureaucrat Deepti Gaur Mukerjee has been appointed as the new Higher Education Secretary as part of a top-level bureaucratic reshuffle carried out by the Centre on Monday. She succeeds Vineet Joshi, who was appointed Secretary in the Ministry of Panchayati Raj last month.

The Personnel Ministry said late on Monday night that the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet had approved Mukerjee's appointment in a partial modification of its July 23 order. The appointment comes in the wake of the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) paper leak controversy.

Following the latest changes, Youth Affairs Secretary Pallavi Jain Govil will be the new Corporate Affairs Secretary in place of Mukerjee. Sunil Paliwal, Chairman of the Inland Waterways Authority of India, has been appointed Youth Affairs Secretary in place of Govil, while Sushil Kumar Lohani, Officer on Special Duty in the Cabinet Secretariat, will succeed Paliwal as Chairman of the Inland Waterways Authority of India.

In another change, V L Kantha Rao, Secretary in the Department of Water Resources, River Development and Ganga Rejuvenation, has been appointed Officer on Special Duty in the Department of Official Language in the Ministry of Home Affairs. Cash row: Justice Yashwant Varma inquiry report to be tabled in Parliament today

The enquiry report into allegations against former judge Justice Yashwant Varma will be tabled in both Houses of Parliament on Wednesday. The move sharpens the constitutional question of whether removal proceedings can continue after his resignation.

The enquiry report into allegations against former Allahabad High Court judge Justice Yashwant Varma will be tabled in the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha on Wednesday, bringing a controversial case involving the alleged discovery of burnt currency at his official residence to a crucial stage.

The three-member enquiry committee, constituted by Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, investigated allegations against Justice Varma following the discovery of burnt currency notes at his official residence in Delhi in March 2025.

Following the incident, Justice Varma was transferred from the Delhi High Court to the Allahabad High Court, and his judicial work was withdrawn pending an in-house enquiry. He resigned from the Allahabad High Court on April 9, 2026, while the parliamentary inquiry was underway.
The resignation has raised a key legal and constitutional question over whether Parliament can continue with removal proceedings against a judge who has resigned while the process is pending.

The parliamentary inquiry committee submitted its report to Speaker Om Birla on May 18. The committee was reconstituted in February and comprises Supreme Court Justice Aravind Kumar, Bombay High Court Chief Justice Shree Chandrashekhar and senior advocate B V Acharya.
The proceedings originated after a removal motion signed by 146 MPs was submitted to the Lok Sabha Speaker in July 2025.
WHAT IS THE ALLEGATION AGAINST JUSTICE VARMA?
The controversy dates back to March 2025, when a fire broke out at Justice Varma's official residence in Delhi. During firefighting operations, burnt currency notes were allegedly found at the site.

Justice Varma has denied the allegations and maintained that no cash was recovered from his residence. He was not present at the residence when the fire broke out and subsequently questioned the basis for holding him responsible for what happened at the premises.

Following the incident, then Chief Justice of India Sanjiv Khanna ordered an in-house inquiry. The panel reportedly found prima facie that Justice Varma and his family had control over the room where the cash was allegedly found.

In August 2025, Speaker Om Birla constituted a three-member committee under the Judges (Inquiry) Act to examine the allegations. Justice Varma later challenged the validity of the parliamentary inquiry before the Supreme Court. The proceedings were ultimately allowed to continue.
The committee completed its proceedings after Justice Varma resigned on April 9 and subsequently submitted its report to the Speaker on May 18.
The report will now be placed before Parliament. Its findings could determine what further parliamentary action is considered in the case.
CAN PARLIAMENT REMOVE A JUDGE AFTER RESIGNATION?
This is the central constitutional question surrounding the case.

Under Articles 124 and 217 of the Constitution, a High Court judge can be removed on grounds of "proved misbehaviour" or "incapacity". The removal process requires an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by at least two-thirds of members present and voting, followed by an order of the President.
Justice Varma's resignation, however, has created an unusual situation because the parliamentary removal process was already underway when he stepped down.

China on Wednesday sought to play down reports of a military standoff with India in the Arunachal Pradesh sector of the Line of Actual Control (LAC), with a foreign ministry spokesperson saying the “border situation is generally stable”.

RSS wing seeks bans, boycott of US firms for tariffs over Russian oil purchase
The SJM’s statement came weeks ahead of RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat’s visit to the US and Canada as part of an international outreach

Swadeshi Jagaran Manch (SJM), the economic wing of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)’s ideological fount, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), criticised the US Senate legislation authorising US President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries making significant purchases of Russian oil and urged the Indian government to stand firm on purchasing it. It asked people to boycott US companies and the government to “impose a unilateral ban” on US tech and social media firms.

India was named as one of five target economies by the bill’s sponsors as the US Senate on Friday approved by 86 votes to 11 the bill. The bill spares US allies in Europe for similar purchases of Russian oil, gas and other exports.

The SJM’s statement came weeks ahead of RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat’s visit to the US and Canada as part of the organisation’s international outreach. “India has time and again made it clear that our sovereign right to purchase energy from legitimate international markets cannot be dictated by any third country…” said SJM national co-convener Ashwani Mahajan in the statement.

He added that India’s decision to buy crude oil from Russia is based on considerations of energy security, availability, price, diversification of supplies and the interests of Indian consumers. He added that if the US has differences with Russia, it is entitled to pursue its own foreign-policy objectives. “However, those objectives should not be converted into unilateral economic coercion against sovereign countries such as India; and tariffs cannot become an instrument of geopolitical coercion,” he said.

The statement said that while US legislation has yet to complete the full process and that tariffs would not be imposed automatically, it clearly poses a serious threat to the principles of free and fair international trade and to the sovereign right of nations to determine their energy policies.

The SJM, which has campaigned for indigenisation and opposed foreign direct investment in key sectors and strategic disinvestment, pointed out that this is not the first time there have been threats to impose unfair tariffs. It added that such threats have persisted since the beginning of Trump’s second term.
Steep tariffs on Indian goods entering the US will significantly impact exports. India is among the largest buyers of Russian oil, and the quantum of purchase has increased since the Iran-US war.

SJM referred to the previous tariffs and said they have been labelled in various ways, ranging from reciprocal tariffs and national security tariffs to Section 301 tariffs, Section 232 tariffs, punitive tariffs (for purchasing Russian oil), trade deficit tariffs, and forced labour tariffs. It said the list is never-ending. “India has clearly stated that its purchase of crude oil from Russia is based on considerations of energy security, availability, pricing, supply diversification, and the interests of Indian consumers.”

SJM expressed concern over what is described as unethical use of tariffs as an instrument of foreign policy. It labelled the Russia-Ukraine war as nothing but a power tussle between NATO, a bloc of western countries, and the Commonwealth of Independent States, an intergovernmental association formed in 1991 after the dissolution of the USSR. SJM added that Western nations are trying to push Ukraine to join NATO. It said sanctions on oil purchases from Russia are only a pressure tactic being used to give effect to its designs.

SJM called on India to remain uncompromising on the issue of energy security. “India’s energy policy must therefore be determined by India’s national interest, and not by external political pressure.”

“The US India trade negotiations cannot be conducted on gunpoint…The latest US legislation assumes particular significance because India and the United States are simultaneously engaged in negotiations on a bilateral trade agreement. The SJM believes that trade negotiations between two sovereign countries must take place on the basis of mutual respect, reciprocity and equality, and not through threats of punitive tariffs,” Mahajan said.

SJM urged the government to withdraw the notification allowing FDI in e-commerce entities, such as Amazon, Flipkart-Walmart, and to hold inventories for exports. It sought the withholding of the bill passed in the Lok Sabha, permitting banks and other electronic service providers to impose Merchant Discount Rate.
SJM demanded that Visa and Mastercard be forbidden to regain a foothold in India and unequivocally rejected any attempt to use US tariffs to dictate India’s oil purchases.

4 Domino's outlets sealed in Maharashtra over food safety violations after FDA raids

The FDA inspected a total of 104 establishments belonging to brands including Domino's Pizza, KFC, Pizza Hut, McDonald's, Subway, Burger King, Starbucks and Monginis. During the drive, operations at two establishments were halted immediately, while 95 improvement notices were issued and five food business licences were suspended with immediate effect.

The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has suspended the food business licences of four Domino’s Pizza outlets after finding multiple food safety and hygiene violations during a special inspection drive across the state.

Three of the affected Domino’s outlets are located in Mumbai, while the fourth is in Satara district. The inspections were carried out on August 11 as part of a statewide drive targeting establishments operated by major restaurant chains.

The FDA inspected a total of 104 establishments belonging to brands including Domino’s Pizza, KFC, Pizza Hut, McDonald’s, Subway, Burger King, Starbucks and Monginis. During the drive, operations at two establishments were halted immediately, while 95 improvement notices were issued and five food business licences were suspended with immediate effect.

In Mumbai, the licence of the Domino’s outlet operated by Jubilant FoodWorks Ltd at Vile Parle West was suspended after inspectors found violations of Schedule 4 of the Food Safety and Standards (Licensing and Registration of Food Businesses) Regulations, 2011.

The FDA flagged deficiencies related to the display of the FSSAI licence, potable water testing, food storage, pest control and hygiene facilities. The outlet was also directed to ensure proper temperature storage and monitoring of frozen and other food products.

Inspectors also found issues with the segregation and disposal of food and non-food items. Repairs were required to the kitchen back door, flooring and chilling room, while measures were ordered to prevent the entry of rodents and other pests.
The FDA further directed the outlet to provide adequate facilities for food preparation, equipment sanitisation and hand-washing and hygiene for food handlers.

Another Domino’s outlet in Borivali West was also found non-compliant, with the inspection report assigning it a 54 per cent compliance score. The FDA cited deficiencies involving food storage, temperature monitoring, food testing, hygiene and pest control.
The outlet was directed to maintain proper segregation between raw and cooked food as well as vegetarian and non-vegetarian food. Raw materials and non-food items must also be stored separately.

Inspectors additionally found a need for better cleaning and sanitisation of equipment and utensils, with oily residue and food scraps in the pizza preparation area required to be removed immediately. Improvements were also ordered in flooring, lighting and overall cleanliness, along with effective pest-control measures.
The third Mumbai Domino’s outlet, located at R-City Mall in Ghatkopar West, also had its licence suspended.

According to the FDA, the establishment lacked proper hygiene and sanitation arrangements and did not maintain a cleaning and sanitation schedule. Inspectors also reported pest infestation and inadequate pest-control measures and records.
The Satara outlet, on the other hand, was found to have a compliance score of 47 per cent.

The FDA cited deficiencies in infrastructure, equipment, cleanliness and pest control. The establishment was directed to introduce proper rack and storage systems for raw food items and conduct laboratory testing of food products while maintaining the required records.
The latest action comes a day after the FDA's crackdown on a Blinkit store in Mumbai's Malad West highlighted serious hygiene and food-storage violations.

During an inspection of the quick-commerce company's facility on August 7, FDA officials found a large number of cockroaches on fruit and vegetable stock. Food items were allegedly being stored directly on the floor, while some racks were rusty and cold-storage areas were poorly maintained.

The inspection also found inadequate pest- and rodent-control measures, expired food products and damaged or apparently tampered-with packages. The store was also not properly following FIFO (First In, First Out) and FEFO (First Expiry, First Out) systems for food storage.

Officials further flagged poor waste management and shortcomings in the personal hygiene of food handlers, including inadequate medical examination and health records and insufficient personal protective equipment.

Following the inspection, the FDA suspended the food licence of Blink Commerce Private Limited under Section 32(3) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The order directed the establishment to keep its food business operations suspended until further instructions.

The Blinkit action was part of a broader food-safety enforcement drive in Maharashtra. Between May 25 and July 31, the FDA inspected 3,137 hotels, restaurants, eateries and other food establishments across Mumbai, issuing 764 improvement notices and suspending 165 licences. The department also seized or destroyed food products weighing 28.66 lakh kg and valued at Rs 55.72 crore, according to FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe.

FCRA bill sent to JPC amid Opposition uproar, Amit Shah’s debate offer rejected: 'We are ready vs man lacks courage'
The FCRA amendment bill was referred to a 31-member JPC amid Opposition protests, while Amit Shah’s offer to discuss student protests was rejected.

A bill proposing controversial amendments to India’s foreign contribution law was referred to a 31-member joint committee of Parliament on Wednesday amid a standoff between the government and the Opposition and repeated disruptions in the House.

The penultimate day of the monsoon session began with Union home minister Amit Shah saying he was ready for a discussion on students’ protests and police action, only for the Opposition – which has been demanding his statement in the House and another debate on the Ram Temple donation row – to rebuff the offer.

“Prime Minister Narendra Modi-led NDA government is ready for discussions. The House should be allowed to run, the Opposition should submit a letter to the speaker by 2pm today. We are ready to start discussion at 3pm today,” Shah said in a rare media interaction outside Parliament.
Also read: FCRA amendments: What the new bill proposes, and why it has sparked pushback
Opposition rejects Shah’s offer for Parliament debate

Shah also wrote to Lok Sabha speaker Om Birla conveying the government’s readiness to participate in the discussion, only for Congress leader Rahul Gandhi to call it a “last-minute attempt” and say that the Opposition was not interested in listening to Shah’s lecture.
The monsoon session is set to end on Thursday. The government indicated that it will not be extended and added that the Opposition’s views will be sought.

Introduced in the previous session but held back at the time, the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill triggered major controversy with the Opposition, several church delegations and three chief ministers of Christian-majority states raising concerns.
31-member panel to examine contentious amendments

Minister of state for home affairs Nityanand Rai and not Shah, as originally listed in the supplementary list of business introduced a resolution in the Lok Sabha on Wednesday afternoon to form the 31-member JPC with 21 Lok Sabha members and 10 Rajya Sabha members. A Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) member is expected to lead the panel.

The Opposition, which tried to pressurise the government to scrap the bill said it will join the JPC. “Even in the JPC, we will continue to strongly oppose this bill and will not allow these unconstitutional and coercive provisions to become law,” said Congress general secretary KC Venugopal.

“On one side, the RSS is getting donations from foreign countries, while on the other side, the government is trying to target minorities and NGOs. The government should withdraw this bill,” he added.
Also read: Centre eyes consensus on sending foreign funding bill to JPC amid demands for complete withdrawal
Rijiju defends JPC move, accuses Opposition of avoiding debate
Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju hit back, saying that the Congress and others had been demanding for days that the bill be referred to a JPC.

“Yet, even when we are referring such an important bill (to a panel), these people have objections. If KC Venugopal or a member of any other party finds anything objectionable in this bill, or if there is any point they wish to oppose, they can present their views in the JPC. The JPC will have sufficient time; hearings will be held, and other people will also be invited to participate. Instead of being pleased about this, they are speaking against it.”
The minister denied any pressure on the government to refer the contentious bill to a House panel and argued that the decision was taken to allow extensive discussion.
Later in the day, he attacked the Opposition.
Also read: FCRA bill may impact Christian groups, Nagaland CM tells Amit Shah
Shah, Gandhi trade sharp remarks over student protests

“I am totally frustrated. For the first time in my life, I am witnessing a scenario where the government wants a discussion in Parliament, yet the Opposition is running away from it. It is hard to imagine this, because in a parliamentary democracy, it is the Opposition that demands a discussion while the government provides the answers,” Rijiju told reporters.

“We are saying that if the Congress states even tomorrow morning at 11:00am that they are ready for the discussion, we will extend the time. You should ask Congress why they got scared and why they fled,” he added.

He also referred to Shah’s letter to Birla, where the home minister said that Rijiju – on behalf of the government during the business advisory committee meeting – gave consent for a discussion in Parliament on student protests.

“I would also like to mention that earlier, at the request of the Opposition, a discussion has already taken place in the current session of Parliament on the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026, in which no honourable Member of Parliament from the Opposition expressed any views in the House regarding the NEET examination. Despite this, the government is ready to discuss this issue once again,” Shah said in the letter written in Hindi.

The minister has asserted that he wanted to be present in the House during the scheduled time to participate in the discussion and was ready to answer all questions. “Solutions emerge only through discussion and dialogue in a democracy. I have unwavering faith in democracy and democratic institutions, and it is my belief that this House is meant precisely for discussion and dialogue,” he wrote.

But the Opposition dismissed the offer. Gandhi alleged that Shah lacked the courage to come to Parliament, reiterating the demand that Shah come to the House and speak on police excesses at Jantar Mantar.

“The Opposition has clearly said that we are not interested in Amit Shah giving us a lecture. When I say ‘we’, I mean the younger generation of this country. Who shot the students? Who gave the order to beat up the students with lathis with nails? Did Amit Shah give this order to shoot our children? If he did, then he should resign. For the last 20 days, Amit Shah has been missing. The home minister of India has no courage; he cannot come to the House,” Gandhi said.
“When a man lacks the courage to speak the truth, his silence speaks for him. Amit Shah’s silence is his confession,” he added.
Formed to review a bill, a joint committee of Parliament initially gets three months’ time but is allowed extensions. Currently, Parliament has 18 such panels.

The bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha in the previous session but was not brought for passage after protests by the Opposition and controversy in then poll-bound Kerala. The bill had evoked sharp reactions from Opposition leaders, particularly Kerala lawmakers, as Christian groups alleged they might be targeted under the new law.
Also read: Nagaland CM urges Shah to reconsider FCRA amendments, seeks parliamentary panel review
Bill proposes wider government control over NGO assets

The amendments establish a designated authority for “a comprehensive framework for vesting, supervision, management and disposal of foreign contribution and assets, including provisional and permanent vesting.” A provision stated that the government can appoint a “designated authority” to take over, manage, or sell assets created from foreign funds by a non-governmental organisation whose licence under FCRA was cancelled, suspended, or simply not renewed.

The bill plans to do away with section 15 of the current act that limits the scope of the authority to manage the activities of the organisation, utilise foreign contribution or dispose of the assets created out of it, in case adequate funds are not available for running such an activity.

In the meeting of opposition parties on Wednesday morning, it was decided that the parties will participate in the JPC panel and not repeat their boycott of the panel on the set of bills to automatically remove ministers if arrested for 30 days. Congress leader Jairam Ramesh said he told the opposition leaders, “We can’t repeat the same mistake”.

The Swadeshi Jagaran Manch (SJM), the economic wing of the Rashtriya Swayamsewak Sangh (RSS), urged the Central Government on Wednesday (August 12, 2026) to remain firm on India’s energy policy and reject all attempts by the United States to use tariffs as leverage over New Delhi’s purchase of Russian crude oil.
The organisation was reacting to recent U.S. Senate legislation that would authorise the U.S. President to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries making significant purchases of Russian oil.

“SJM fully supports the Government of India’s stand on the issue that India’s purchase of Russian crude oil is based on considerations of energy security, availability, price, diversification of supplies and the interests of Indian consumers. India has time and again made it clear that our sovereign right to purchase energy from legitimate international markets cannot be dictated by any third country,” said SJM National Co Convener, Ashwani Mahajan.

He added that the unilateral tariffs could undermine free and fair international trade and create uncertainty for exporters, importers, investors and consumers. He also argued that Russian crude has helped diversify India’s oil supplies and contain energy costs.

The organisation linked the proposed tariff measures to ongoing India-U.S. trade negotiations, arguing that discussions between the two countries should be based on equality, reciprocity and mutual respect rather than the threat of punitive duties.

“If one powerful country is allowed to impose punitive tariffs on another country for buying goods from a third country, the principle of sovereign economic decision-making itself comes under threat,” said Mr. Mahajan.

He also criticised recent policy changes concerning foreign investment in e-commerce and the proposed framework allowing banks and payment providers to levy merchant discount rate (MDR) on UPI transactions. He claimed the measures could benefit U.S.-based companies and weaken Indian businesses and digital-payment platforms.

Calling for a stronger response to Washington’s actions, SJM urged the government to reconsider the e-commerce policy change, withhold the MDR-related legislation, and reject any demand affecting India’s agriculture, dairy sector, energy security or strategic autonomy.
The organisation also called for a boycott of American products and services.

“Boycott products like Pepsi and Coke, social media firms, and e-Commerce platforms belonging to U.S. companies, to start with. If the U.S. continues to act against India’s interests, this boycott can be extended to services of other U.S. giants as well,” said Mr. Mahajan.

Kerala govt may order probe into previous LDF's Messi, Argentina visit proposal

Kerala ministers have accused the previous government of procedural lapses in the failed Messi event plan. The row has widened into questions over public spending, sponsor selection and misuse of official machinery.

The UDF government in Kerala is likely to order a probe into alleged irregularities and procedural lapses in the previous Left government's attempt to bring football legend Lionel Messi and the Argentina team to the state. Sports Minister O J Janeesh on Wednesday rejected former minister V Abdurahiman's defence of the proposal and alleged that official machinery was used to help a private individual make financial gains.

Later in the day, Health and Devaswom Minister K Muraleedharan also said the government would order an investigation into the campaign around Messi's proposed visit and the renovation of a stadium in its name. The remarks came a day after Janeesh said the Sports Department had submitted its inquiry report on the controversy to the government for further action.

Janeesh said there was no substance in Abdurahiman's claim that the government had not suffered any financial loss in connection with the proposed event. He alleged that official procedures were not followed from the start and that there was no transparency in selecting the sponsor and handling the proposal.

"The government machinery was misused for a private event management company. From the Chief Secretary to the district collector, police and Greater Cochin Development Authority (GCDA), the administrative machinery was used for a private individual," Janeesh alleged while speaking to reporters. He said this created an opportunity for a private party to make substantial financial gains and, therefore, it was meaningless to argue that the government had suffered no loss.

The minister said the first email proposing the event was received by the then sports minister from an advertising company that had been registered only about 20 days earlier. He said the company had a capital of only Rs 1 lakh and questioned whether its background, financial capacity and experience to organise an event involving Messi and the Argentina team had been examined.

Janeesh alleged that the proposal was not handled according to the prescribed Rules of Procedure. He said the communication remained outside the official file system for nearly two years without being registered or given a file number. "It is clear that there were individual interests. The former sports minister's action in this regard amounts to a serious violation of the oath of office," he alleged, adding that official procedures for correspondence with private individuals and institutions should have been followed.

He also questioned the purpose of Abdurahiman's trip to Spain in connection with the proposal and said there should be greater clarity on that visit as well as on the selection of the sponsor. Janeesh alleged that the previous minister had communicated with private parties through his personal email for nearly two years before bringing the matter into official files, and said the government had a legal and constitutional responsibility in dealing with such matters.

The minister said around Rs 14 lakh of government money had been spent, including on the Spain visit, and that this should also be treated as a loss. He also referred to reports that Rs 126 crore provided by the sponsor had been lost and said clarity was needed on where that money went. Janeesh further questioned former Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan's earlier statement assuring Kerala that Messi would come to the state, asking whether he was aware of the developments that had now come to light.

Muraleedharan said the government would act over the matter. "We will definitely bring before the law those who spent crores in the name of Messi, who never came. There is no doubt about it. We will bring out the truth, including the alleged corruption in the stadium renovation, for which Rs 75 crore was spent," he told reporters. He said the facts would come out and the government would not be deterred by false propaganda, adding that the then chief minister would also have to answer questions on the issue.
Janeesh had said the inquiry report was prepared by the Sports Department Special Secretary after examining files available with the department and had been handed over to the government.

Abdurahiman, however, has rejected the allegations and said the LDF government followed all prescribed procedures while trying to bring the Argentina team to Kerala for a friendly match. In a detailed statement, he said the state government did not suffer even a single rupee of loss because the agreement for the match was between the Argentina Football Association and the sponsor and imposed no financial liability on the government.
Karnataka says releasing 12,000 cusecs of Cauvery water to Tamil Nadu difficult
Karnataka has said it will be difficult to release 12,000 cusecs of Cauvery water daily to Tamil Nadu. The state will place its objections before the Supreme Court as protests gather pace.

Karnataka Minister Ramalinga Reddy on Wednesday said the state would find it difficult to release 12,000 cusecs of Cauvery water a day to Tamil Nadu, as directed by the Cauvery Water Management Authority.

He said the state government would decide its next course of action after a Supreme Court hearing on Thursday on Tamil Nadu's petition, and added that it would ensure that no injustice was done to Karnataka.

The Cauvery Water Regulation Committee, which met in New Delhi on Tuesday, directed Karnataka to release 12,000 cusecs of water daily to Tamil Nadu for 15 days from August 12. The Cauvery Water Management Authority later upheld the decision.

Reddy said discussions had been held with Chief Minister D K Shivakumar and officials. “I have held discussions with the Chief Minister (D K Shivakumar) and officials. The CM spoke to our Advocate General and advocates in Delhi. Tamil Nadu's petition is coming up before the Supreme Court tomorrow; it has been listed. We will have an opportunity there, and our advocates will file our objections. Let's see what the Supreme Court says. Thereafter, we will have further options,” he said.

Speaking to reporters, the State Water Resources Minister said the government's future course of action would depend on the outcome of the hearing. “Tamil Nadu has filed a petition, and we have been served a notice. We will have an opportunity to present our case there. Based on the outcome, we will decide whether further legal action is required. This is based on the suggestions given by the advocates,” he added.

The Tamil Nadu government had earlier this month moved the Supreme Court over the Cauvery dispute with Karnataka, saying that the quantum of water directed by the CWRC, as well as the water released by Karnataka, was insufficient.

Earlier, on July 28, the CWRC had directed Karnataka to release 3,500 cusecs of Cauvery water to Tamil Nadu for 15 days. Karnataka had initially said it could not release water because of poor storage in its reservoirs. However, after heavy rain in the Cauvery catchment areas in the state, it began releasing water under the earlier 3,500-cusec direction.

Reddy said Karnataka had complied with that earlier order and had, in fact, released more water to Tamil Nadu. “When the Kabini dam filled due to rains in the catchment area, the water flowed downstream as there was no scope to store it further. About 10 TMC of water has flown,” he said.

He said Karnataka had about 76 TMC of water in its reservoirs, of which 36 TMC would be needed every year for drinking water, apart from losses due to evaporation and the requirement for rivers and crops. “We have about 76 TMC of water (in our dams), out of which we will need 36 TMC a year for drinking water. There will also be evaporation, and we will have to release water to rivers and for crops. Asking Karnataka to release 12,000 cusecs for 15 days is inappropriate,” he said.

Reddy said the earlier direction to release 3,500 cusecs a day was somewhat acceptable, but the latest order to release 12,000 cusecs daily for 15 days, amounting to about 16 TMC, was “too costly” for Karnataka. He said the state would not have faced difficulty if it had been asked to release a smaller quantity. “This is too high a quantity,” he said.

He also said the monsoon had not been satisfactory in Karnataka's old Mysuru region and claimed that Tamil Nadu had enough water in its reservoirs. He said Tamil Nadu receives most of its rainfall during the northeast monsoon from October to December and has a better water table than Karnataka. “Our water table is too low here. Even if we go 800-1,000 feet, we don't get water, while they get water at much higher levels. Despite our Additional Chief Secretary, advocates, and experts effectively putting forward our case with all these facts, the order has come. It will be difficult for us to release 16 TMC of water in 15 days. We have discussed it. We will decide what to do,” he said.
“The CM has spoken to advocates in New Delhi and experts. We will ensure that no injustice happens to the state,” he added.

Meanwhile, farmers have staged sporadic protests in Cauvery basin districts, including Mandya and Mysuru, against the water release order. Some pro-Kannada organisations have called for a Karnataka bandh on Thursday in protest against the directive, while others have opposed the bandh call. Overall, the state government has said it will place its objections before the Supreme Court and decide its next steps after the hearing.

With Tamil Nadu realising a little over 4.5 thousand million cubic feet (tmc ft.) as mandated by the the Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA) and the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee (CWRC) this month, the two bodies are holding their meetings on Tuesday to take stock of the situation.

As on August 6, for which the data released by the Central Water Commission (CWC) are available, the lower riparian State realised about 4.6 tmc ft in the current month. Cumulatively (since June 1), the total amount of quantum received was around 8.3 tmc ft. In a normal year, the State should have got around 49 tmc ft. till now.

On July 28, the CWRC directed Karnataka to ensure that Tamil Nadu realised, at Biligundlu (the gauge and discharge (G&D) site being used by the CWC on the inter-State border), 3,500 cubic feet per second (cusecs) of water for 15 days, starting from July 29. Two days later, the CWMA endorsed the Committee’s decision.

As on date, the combined storage of four reservoirs in Karnataka was around 88 tmc ft. against the total capacity of 114.57 tmc ft. In the last two-odd months, the reservoirs have cumulatively received 77.75 tmc ft. and discharged 21.46 tmc ft. As for the Mettur dam in Tamil Nadu, the storage was 40.35 tmc ft. against the capacity of 93.47 tmc ft.
